period: Settled since prehistory; oracle famous from the 6th century BC; Shali founded 1203
summary: A green island 19 metres below sea level, 50 km from Libya, where people speak a Berber language and the ancient world came to ask Amun the future.
look: Siwa is a long hollow in the desert, about 80 km from end to end and up to 20 km wide, sunk below sea level between the Qattara Depression and the Great Sand Sea. Around you: walled palm gardens, about 200 springs, two big salt lakes and limestone hills full of tombs. The ruined mud town of Shali stands in the middle of modern Siwa; the oracle temple at Aghurmi is a few km east, Gebel al-Mawta just north.
story:
No other place in Egypt is quite like it. The oasis lies 560 km from Cairo and only 50 km from the Libyan border, in a depression about 19 metres below sea level. Water rises from roughly 200 springs and feeds around 300,000 date palms and some 70,000 olive trees. The ancient Egyptians called it the Field of Trees; Greeks and Romans called it Ammonium, after its god.

That god, Amun, made Siwa famous. From the 6th century BC Greeks from Cyrene, a king of Lydia and generals from Sparta and Athens sent envoys to his oracle, and in 331 BC Alexander the Great came in person. Then the oasis slipped out of history. Medieval Arab geographers mention it, and the first European to describe it since Roman times was William George Browne in 1792. Muhammad Ali annexed Siwa to Egypt in 1820, and the Siwans did not take it quietly: an Egyptian official was murdered here in 1838.

Most of the roughly 25,000 to 30,000 people are Amazigh, or Berbers, who call themselves and their home Isiwan. Their language, Siwi, is the easternmost Berber language. Until a paved road reached the Mediterranean coast in the 1980s, the oasis lived largely by its own rules: marriage mostly within the community, strong clans, a religious and conservative way of life that still shapes the streets. You will see few women in public.

A good day: the oracle temple in the cool morning, the painted tombs of Gebel al-Mawta, a swim at Cleopatra's Spring, Shali in the late afternoon and sunset over the salt lake at Fatnas. Dates and olive oil pay the bills; tourism is the newer crop.
details: In the old lanes around Shali: walls of kershef, salty lake mud with palm-trunk beams, the stuff the whole old town was built from.
Women's grey-blue tarfottet shawls: a Siwan signature. Please do not photograph women, even from a distance.
Garden walls of mud brick with small channels of spring water running along them into the palm groves.
Donkey carts sharing the road with tuk-tuks: both are normal transport here.
To the west, the pale sheen of Birket Siwa, the salt lake, fringed with white crust.
fun_fact: The chemical word 'ammonia' comes from here: Roman writers said sal ammoniac, the 'salt of Ammon', was found near the god's temple in this oasis.
narration: You are in Siwa, the westernmost oasis of Egypt, about 560 kilometres from Cairo and only 50 from the Libyan border. The whole oasis sits in a hollow about 19 metres below sea level. Water rises from roughly 200 springs and feeds around 300,000 date palms and 70,000 olive trees, all wrapped in sand and salt lakes. The ancient Egyptians called it the Field of Trees. The Greeks called it Ammonium, after its god, because this was the home of the Oracle of Amun, consulted by Greek cities and kings and, in 331 BC, by Alexander the Great himself. The people are Amazigh, or Berbers. They call themselves Isiwan, and among themselves they speak Siwi, the easternmost Berber language in the world, closer to Libya than to Cairo. Until a paved road arrived in the 1980s, the oasis lived almost on its own, and it is still conservative and close-knit. Dress modestly, and do not photograph women. In a day you can see the oracle temple at Aghurmi, the painted tombs on the Mountain of the Dead, a spring for a swim, the melted mud town of Shali, and sunset over the salt lake. Now look for the old town in the middle of the new one: that crumbling, sand-coloured hill full of holes is Shali, a whole town built of salt and mud.

period: Ancient Paraetonium; Alexander passed in 331 BC; battles of 1942
summary: Alexander's jumping-off point for the oracle, Mark Antony's refuge after Actium, Rommel's seaside cave: the last town before 300 km of nothing.
look: Marsa Matruh is a port and summer resort on a wide bay of white sand and clear, pale water, about 240 km west of Alexandria. A line of rocks across the bay acts as a natural breakwater. From here the Siwa road turns south and runs about 300 km over an empty stony plateau before dropping into the oasis.
story:
Long before the beach hotels, this was a harbour. Ramesses II had a temple here around 1200 BC, and the Greeks and Romans called the town Paraetonium. In early 331 BC Alexander the Great marched west along this coast from his newly founded Alexandria, reached Paraetonium, and turned inland across the desert toward the oracle of Amun at Siwa.

Under the Romans the port shipped Egyptian grain to Rome. Its most famous visitor came in defeat: after losing the battle of Actium in 31 BC, Mark Antony landed at Paraetonium. Local legend goes further and says Cleopatra bathed with him in a rock pool on the coast west of town, still called Cleopatra's Bath. No ancient writer mentions the pool, but the story has outlived every sceptic.

In June 1942 Rommel's Afrika Korps captured Matruh at the Battle of Mersa Matruh, and the Allies took it back after El Alamein that November. A rock-cut cave on the east side of the bay, where tradition says Rommel drew up his plans, is now a small military museum.

Then the sea is behind you. The road climbs onto a flat gravel plateau with a few Bedouin settlements and roadside cafés, and near the end drops down an escarpment to the first palms of Siwa.
details: The line of rocks across the mouth of the bay: a natural breakwater with a small gap for boats.
Cleopatra's Bath, west of town: a hollow in the shore rocks where the waves surge in. Look, but swim only if the sea is calm.
Rommel's cave museum on the east side of the bay: cool rock-cut rooms with wartime maps, photos and objects.
On the road south: the green coastal strip gives way to bare stony plateau soon after you leave town.
Near the end of the drive, the road descends an escarpment and the first dark line of palms appears below.
fun_fact: Arrian says Alexander's march from Alexandria to Paraetonium was 1,600 stades long, and on the way into the desert his army ran out of water; you have air-conditioning.
narration: This is Marsa Matruh, a white-sand bay on the Mediterranean and the last real town before Siwa. In antiquity it was Paraetonium, a harbour that shipped Egyptian grain to Rome. In early 331 BC Alexander the Great marched along this coast from his brand-new Alexandria, reached Paraetonium, and turned south into the desert to consult the oracle of Amun. You are following his route. Three centuries later Mark Antony landed here after his defeat at Actium, and local legend says Cleopatra bathed with him in a rock pool west of town, still called Cleopatra's Bath. No ancient writer mentions the pool, but the story refuses to die. In June 1942 Rommel's Afrika Korps captured the town, and a seaside cave where he is said to have planned his attacks is now a small museum. From here the road runs about 300 kilometres south over a flat, stony plateau with almost nothing on it. Watch the end of the drive: the road drops down an escarpment, and the first dark line of palm trees appears below you.

summary: From 1940 to 1942 this coast was the front line of the desert war, and parts of the desert still hide its mines.
look: There is nothing of the war to see in Siwa itself; the traces are on the coast. Rommel's cave museum is at Marsa Matruh, and El Alamein, with its war cemeteries and museum, lies further east toward Alexandria.
story:
From 1940 to early 1943 Italian, German, British and Commonwealth armies chased each other back and forth along this coast. Erwin Rommel, the 'Desert Fox', took Marsa Matruh in June 1942 and was stopped at El Alamein, where the cliffs of the Qattara Depression protected the Allied southern flank. Bernard Montgomery's offensive there began on 23 October 1942 and turned the war in Africa.

Siwa saw a quieter war. The British Long Range Desert Group used it as a base for raids far behind enemy lines, and Axis troops, including an Italian division, held the oasis for a time in 1942. Both sides laid vast minefields, the 'Devil's Gardens'. Many were never fully cleared, which is why desert drivers stick to known tracks.
details: Rusted metal in the sand anywhere in the desert: leave it alone and tell your driver.
Your driver's route: notice how he follows existing tyre tracks rather than cutting fresh ones.
On the coast road east of Matruh: signs for the El Alamein war cemeteries and memorials.
fun_fact: The Second Battle of El Alamein began on the night of 23 October 1942: on the 23rd of your trip it will be exactly 84 years.
narration: Siwa looks peaceful, but this whole region was a battlefield in the Second World War. From 1940 to 1942, Italian, German, British and Commonwealth armies pushed each other back and forth along the coast. Erwin Rommel, the Desert Fox, took Marsa Matruh in June 1942, and a cave there is now his museum. He was stopped at El Alamein, and Montgomery's offensive there began on 23 October 1942. Siwa itself was a base for the British Long Range Desert Group, and Axis troops held it for a time. Both sides sowed huge minefields, and not all were cleared. So if you see rusted metal in the sand, leave it where it is, and trust your driver's tracks.

summary: A sea of dunes more than half the size of Greece, combed into ridges running north to south: the place 19th-century explorers failed to cross.
look: South of Siwa the palms stop and the dunes begin. You are on the northern edge of an erg of about 72,000 square km that stretches roughly 650 km south along the Libyan border. Long ridges run north to south, separated by flat gravel corridors that the drivers use as roads; from a dune top they look like a frozen swell.
story:
The Great Sand Sea covers about 72,000 square kilometres of western Egypt and eastern Libya, more than half the size of Greece. Satellite images show it combed into long parallel ridges running roughly north to south, some reported to run for over 100 km, with the highest dunes often said to top 100 metres. Between them lie flat corridors of gravel. Caravan traders and oasis people knew how to skirt it; very few tried to cross it.

The first European to try was the German explorer Gerhard Rohlfs. In the winter of 1873-74 his expedition set out west from Dakhla oasis, hoping to reach Kufra in Libya. The dunes beat them. Short of water, they turned north toward Siwa and were saved by a rare desert rainstorm; Rohlfs named the spot Regenfeld, 'rain field', and built a cairn there. He also gave the dunes their name: the Grosse Sandmeer, the Great Sand Sea.

In the late 1920s and 1930s the British officer Ralph Bagnold and his friends learned to drive Ford cars across the sand, with steel channels to climb out of soft patches and a sun compass Bagnold designed himself. Bagnold later founded the Long Range Desert Group and wrote the classic scientific book on how dunes move.

Under the sand lies an old sea floor: around Siwa the rocks are marine limestones, and fossil shells and sea urchins turn up on the gravel. Trips today go by 4x4, ideally in convoy, with permits arranged by your operator. Dune driving is a roller coaster; if it is too much, say so.
details: The flat gravel corridor between two dune ridges: this is the 'road', and it can run straight to the horizon.
Any big dune: a gentle rippled side facing the wind and a steep slip face where the sand avalanches down.
Fossil shells and sea urchins on rocky patches near the oasis edge: photograph them, leave them.
Early morning sand: tiny tracks of beetles and lizards, and sometimes the neat prints of a fennec fox.
At sunset: the sand shifts from pale gold to orange to pink within a few minutes.
fun_fact: A dune field on Mars, explored by NASA's Curiosity rover, is called the Bagnold Dunes, after the officer who learned his trade on these sands.
narration: Ahead of you is the Great Sand Sea, about 72,000 square kilometres of dunes, more than half the size of Greece, stretching south along the Libyan border. From above it looks combed: long ridges running north to south, some for over 100 kilometres, with flat gravel corridors in between that the drivers use as roads. The first European to try to cross it was the German explorer Gerhard Rohlfs. In the winter of 1873 he set out west from Dakhla Oasis, aiming for Kufra in Libya. The dunes beat him. Short of water, his caravan turned north toward Siwa and was saved by a rare rainstorm in the middle of the desert. Rohlfs called the spot Regenfeld, rain field, built a cairn there, and gave this whole sea of sand its name. Half a century later a British officer, Ralph Bagnold, learned to drive Ford cars across it, and later wrote the classic book on how dunes move. A dune field on Mars is named after him. Under the sand lies an old sea floor, and around the edges you may find fossil shells and sea urchins. Please leave them where they are. Now look at the dune nearest you: one side is a gentle ripple, the other a steep slip face where the sand avalanches down. That steep side tells you which way the wind blows.

summary: A hot spring and a cool lake hidden among the dunes: soak at sunset, then watch more stars than you knew existed.
look: About 15 km into the dunes south of Siwa town: a small pool of hot, sulphur-smelling water fed by a pipe from a deep well, and a short walk away a cooler lake edged with reeds. Camps set out carpets and low tables for tea on the dune crest above.
story:
Bir Wahed simply means 'Well One'. Unlike Siwa's ancient springs, it is modern: the water is said to come from a borehole drilled by oil prospectors in the 20th century, who struck hot water instead. The result is a hot pool in the middle of the sand, and nearby a lake of cooler water where the overflow has gathered in a hollow of the dunes.

The ritual is simple. Drivers bring you across the dunes in the afternoon; you soak in the hot pool, then climb the nearest crest for tea as the sun sets over the sand sea. Many groups stay on for dinner at a desert camp.

With no town for many kilometres, the night sky is the real show. In mid-October 2026 the moon is a thin crescent that sets early in the evening, so the Milky Way should be clear overhead.

Bring a swimsuit you do not mind smelling of sulphur, a towel, sandals, a warm layer for after dark, a torch, and a bag to keep sand out of your phone.
details: The hot pool: a faint yellowish film and a smell of eggs. That is sulphur, harmless, but it clings to swimwear.
The cooler lake a short walk away, ringed with reeds: water that spilled from the well and pooled in the dunes.
From the dune crest at sunset, look west: the long parallel ridges of the Great Sand Sea.
After dark, look up: the Milky Way overhead, and Siwa's lights only a faint glow on the horizon.
fun_fact: The men who drilled 'Well One' were hoping for something black and profitable; the desert gave them a hot bath instead.
narration: You are at Bir Wahed, which simply means Well One, about 15 kilometres into the dunes south of Siwa. Unlike the old springs of the oasis, this water is new. It is said to come from a borehole drilled by oil prospectors, who hoped for oil and struck hot water instead. So now there is a hot, sulphur-smelling pool in the middle of the sand, and a short walk away a cooler lake where the overflow has gathered among reeds. The ritual is simple: soak in the hot pool, then climb the nearest dune for tea as the sun drops over the Great Sand Sea. After dark, stay a while. There is no town for many kilometres, and in mid-October the moon is a thin crescent that sets early, so the Milky Way should be clear overhead. Right now, look at the edge of the hot pool: the yellowish film and the smell of eggs are the sulphur at work.

summary: Yellow-green glass scattered on the desert floor by a cosmic impact 29 million years ago, and carved into the scarab on Tutankhamun's chest.
look: You will not find it near Siwa: the glass lies far to the south, between the dune ridges of the southern Great Sand Sea near the Libyan border, several hundred km from here. Pieces range from pebbles to blocks of many kilos, pale yellow to green, wind-polished and often translucent. If a shop in Siwa offers you some, admire it and leave it: it may not leave Egypt.
story:
Libyan desert glass is a natural glass made almost entirely of silica, scattered in fragments over tens of square kilometres of desert in western Egypt and eastern Libya. It formed about 29 million years ago, when something from space struck or exploded above the desert and melted the sand. For decades scientists argued about how. A widely reported 2006 study suggested an airburst, a blast in the air like the one over Tunguska in 1908. More recent work found microscopic zircon structures that, researchers say, only form under the pressures of a real impact.

Stone Age people knapped it into tools. Patrick Clayton of the Egyptian Desert Survey brought it to science in 1932, and in 1933 he and the mineralogist L. J. Spencer described it in a lecture on silica glass from the Libyan Desert.

Its most famous piece is on Tutankhamun's chest. One of his pectorals has a winged scarab at its centre carved from translucent yellow-green stone, and in the 1990s the Italian mineralogist Vincenzo de Michele identified it as desert glass. So more than 3,300 years ago someone carried a lump of it out of the Great Sand Sea to the royal workshops.

Today Egypt protects it, and taking it out of the country is illegal.
details: If you photographed Tutankhamun's jewellery at GEM on the 11th, find the winged-scarab pectoral: the scarab is this glass.
In Siwa shops: pale yellow 'desert glass' for sale. Look, but do not buy it to take home.
On a genuine piece: a pitted, frosted skin from millions of years of sandblasting, clear glass inside.
Inside the glass: tiny bubbles and swirls, signs that it was once molten.
fun_fact: Pure silica only melts at around 1,700 degrees Celsius, far hotter than any ancient furnace: Tutankhamun's jewellers could carve this glass, but never make it.
narration: Picture a scatter of yellow-green glass lying on the sand between the dunes, far to the south of here near the Libyan border. This is Libyan desert glass, almost pure silica, and it formed about 29 million years ago, when something from space struck or exploded over the desert and melted the sand. Scientists still argue whether it was an impact or a blast in the air, though recent studies of tiny zircon crystals point to a real impact. Stone Age people chipped it into tools, and a British surveyor, Patrick Clayton, brought it to science in 1932. But its most famous piece is on Tutankhamun's chest. One of his pectorals has a winged scarab at its centre, and in the 1990s an Italian mineralogist recognised that scarab as desert glass. So, more than 3,300 years ago, someone carried glass made by a cosmic impact out of the Great Sand Sea to the royal workshops. And if a shop in Siwa offers you a piece, admire it, but leave it: taking desert glass out of Egypt is illegal.

summary: Fifty thousand Persian soldiers marched to destroy the oracle and vanished in a sandstorm. Or did they? Nobody has ever found them.
look: There is nothing to see, which is the point. Somewhere in the sand between the southern oases and Siwa, Herodotus says, an entire army lies buried. Stand on a dune, look south-east, and you are looking toward the stretch of desert where the hunters have searched.
story:
The story comes from Herodotus, the Greek historian, who visited Egypt a couple of generations later. Cambyses II, the Persian king who conquered Egypt around 525 BC, sent 50,000 men from Thebes to enslave the Ammonians and burn the oracle of Amun. They reached a town Herodotus calls Oasis, seven days' march across the sand, probably Kharga. After that, he admits, nobody knew anything except what the Ammonians said: that halfway across the desert, while the soldiers were eating, a great and violent south wind arose and buried them all.

The tale has lured adventurers ever since. Laszlo Almasy, the real man behind The English Patient, looked for the army; so did the British officer Orde Wingate in 1933. In 1983-84 an American expedition led by the journalist Gary Chafetz spent six months and about 250,000 dollars with ground radar and an ultralight aircraft. It found some 500 burial mounds, but the bones in them dated to around 1500 BC, a thousand years too early. In 2009 the Italian brothers Angelo and Alfredo Castiglioni announced weapons, a silver bracelet, earrings and human bones near Siwa. They presented them in a documentary rather than a scientific paper, and Zahi Hawass, then head of Egypt's antiquities, called the reports unfounded.

In 2015 Olaf Kaper of Leiden University proposed a cooler answer. Working at Dakhla oasis, he argued that the army was defeated by an Egyptian rebel king, Petubastis III, and that the sandstorm was a convenient story spread later, after Darius the Great crushed the rebels. It is a theory, but many Egyptologists already doubted the storm.

It is easy to see why the tale is loved in Siwa: in it, the oasis' god defends his oracle and the desert does the rest.
details: From any dune top, look south-east: Herodotus puts the disaster somewhere between Kharga and Siwa, in that direction.
Feel the wind: a hot south wind lifting sand is exactly what Herodotus blamed.
The oracle temple on the Aghurmi rock: the army's target, still standing.
Ask your driver about the army: many Siwan guides have a theory, and some claim to know a spot.
fun_fact: The 1980s expedition did find bones under desert mounds, but dating put them around 1500 BC: right desert, wrong millennium.
narration: Somewhere out in this sand, if you believe Herodotus, lie 50,000 Persian soldiers. Around 525 BC the Persian king Cambyses conquered Egypt. Herodotus, the Greek historian who visited a couple of generations later, says Cambyses sent an army from Thebes to enslave the people of this oasis and burn the oracle of Amun. The soldiers marched seven days to another oasis, probably Kharga, and set out across the desert. Then, the Siwans said, while the men were eating, a great and violent south wind arose and buried them all. Nobody saw them again. The story has been catnip for adventurers. Laszlo Almasy, the real man behind The English Patient, looked for them. An American expedition in the 1980s spent six months with radar and a microlight plane, and found only much older graves. In 2009 two Italian brothers announced bones and weapons, but they showed them in a documentary, not a scientific paper, and Egypt's antiquities chief called the claim unfounded. In 2015 the Dutch Egyptologist Olaf Kaper offered another idea: an Egyptian rebel king, Petubastis, defeated the army, and the sandstorm was a cover story spread later. Many Egyptologists think the storm is legend. Now feel the wind on your face. A hot south wind full of sand is still the weather Siwans dread.

period: Late Period, 26th Dynasty, reign of Amasis, 570-526 BC
summary: The oracle that rivalled Delphi: Greek cities, a Spartan general and Alexander the Great climbed this rock to ask Amun about the future.
look: The temple stands on top of the Aghurmi rock, a few km east of Siwa town, inside the ruins of a mud-brick village that grew around it. Walk up through the old village gate; the small stone temple is at the summit: courtyards, a hall, and at the back the narrow sanctuary where the god's image stood. A narrow passage runs beside the sanctuary. Then go to the edge of the rock and look out over the palms.
story:
Amun was probably worshipped at Siwa before this building existed, but the temple you see dates to the 26th Dynasty, and its inscriptions name King Amasis, who ruled 570-526 BC. It is small and plain, and some scholars see Greek touches in its details. Its god was Amun, whom the Greeks identified with Zeus. Through the Greek colony of Cyrene on the Libyan coast, the oracle's fame spread across the Greek world: Zeus Ammon got a temple at Aphytis in Chalkidiki, the poet Pindar wrote him a hymn, and the Cyrenaeans dedicated a chariot with a statue of Ammon at Delphi.

The client list is impressive. Herodotus says Croesus of Lydia sent to this oracle when he tested the great oracles of his day. The Spartan general Lysander is said to have tried to bribe its priests, who reported him. In 449 BC the Athenian Kimon sent envoys with a secret question; the oracle sent them away, saying Kimon was already with the god, and they came home to learn he had died. In 331 BC Alexander the Great came in person.

Siwa did not give riddles in verse; it answered yes or no. In public, about 80 priests carried the god's image in a sacred boat, and the boat answered by tilting toward or away from the questioner. Kings went into the sanctuary alone. Archaeologists found a hidden space next to the sanctuary from which a priest could hear what was asked, which suggests the god had some help.
details: The village gate on the way up: Aghurmi was a fortified village whose houses wrapped around the temple.
The sanctuary at the back: a narrow stone room, with faint carved figures and hieroglyphs on its walls.
The narrow passage beside the sanctuary: stand inside and imagine a priest listening.
From the edge of the rock: the palm groves, the shine of the salt lake and the two humps of Gebel Dakrur to the south.
fun_fact: When Croesus tested the oracles, he asked what he was doing on a set day: he was boiling a tortoise and a lamb in a bronze pot. Delphi got it right; Siwa, Herodotus implies, did not.
narration: You are on the rock of Aghurmi, inside the ruins of a mud-brick village, and the small stone building at the top is the Temple of the Oracle of Amun. It was built in the 6th century BC, under the pharaoh Amasis, and for centuries it was one of the most famous oracles of the ancient world, spoken of in the same breath as Delphi. Greek settlers at Cyrene, on the Libyan coast, spread its fame. The Greeks called the god Zeus Ammon, the poet Pindar wrote him a hymn, and there was even a temple of Zeus Ammon at Aphytis in Chalkidiki. Herodotus says King Croesus of Lydia sent envoys here. The Spartan general Lysander is said to have tried to bribe its priests, and they reported him. And in 331 BC Alexander the Great walked into the sanctuary alone, and came out, he said, with the answer he wanted. Siwa did not speak in riddles. The answers were yes or no. In public processions, priests carried the god in a sacred boat, and the boat tilted to answer. Archaeologists also found a hidden space beside the sanctuary where a priest could hear every question, so the god may have had some help. Now walk to the back, find the narrow passage beside the sanctuary, and imagine standing there in the dark, listening.

summary: A 24-year-old king crossed the desert to ask a god who his father was. He left as 'son of Zeus-Ammon', and later wore the ram's horns to prove it.
look: There is no monument to Alexander in Siwa; the place to stand is the oracle temple on the Aghurmi rock. The narrow sanctuary at the back is where he went in alone, while his companions waited outside on the hilltop.
story:
In the winter of 332-331 BC Alexander, aged 24, had just taken Egypt from the Persians. Instead of chasing the Persian king, he marched west along the coast to Paraetonium, today's Marsa Matruh, and turned south into the desert to consult Amun. Arrian, writing from the memoirs of Alexander's officers, tells the story: the water ran short, then rain fell; when the guides lost the way, two snakes, says Ptolemy, or two ravens, says Aristobulus, led the army to the oasis.

At the temple Alexander entered the sanctuary alone. What he asked, and what he heard, nobody knows. Later writers say the high priest greeted him as son of Amun, the normal title of any pharaoh. Plutarch adds a lovely variant: the priest, trying to be friendly in Greek, meant to say 'O paidion', 'my son', but it came out as 'O pai Dios', 'son of Zeus'. Alexander told his companions only that he had heard what he wished, and wrote to his mother Olympias that he had received secret answers he would tell her in person. He never saw her again.

From then on he called Zeus-Ammon his father. After his death, coins of his successors, most famously Lysimachus, showed him with the curled ram's horns of Ammon. Ancient writers say he wished to be buried here; instead Ptolemy seized the body on its way to Macedonia and took it to Memphis, and later it went to Alexandria, where the tomb was lost.

Siwa never quite let go. In 1995 the Greek archaeologist Liana Souvaltzi announced that she had found Alexander's tomb in the oasis. Experts, Greek and Egyptian, rejected the claim, but you will still hear it in town.
details: The sanctuary door at the back of the oracle temple: the threshold Alexander crossed alone.
The rock's edge outside: where his companions waited, looking over the same palms.
On your phone, a Lysimachus silver coin: the ram's horn curling over Alexander's ear began with this oracle.
In Luxor on the 22nd: Alexander's chapel in Luxor Temple shows him as a pharaoh making offerings to Amun.
fun_fact: In later Arabic and Persian tradition Alexander is often linked with Dhul-Qarnayn, 'the two-horned one'; one theory ties the name to the ram's horns on his coins.
narration: Here, in early 331 BC, Alexander the Great asked a god who his father was. He was 24, and had just taken Egypt from the Persians. Instead of chasing the Persian king, he marched west along the coast to Marsa Matruh and turned into the desert. His officers' memoirs say the water ran out, then rain fell, and when the guides got lost, two snakes, or two ravens, depending on who tells it, led the army to the oasis. At the temple on the Aghurmi rock he went into the sanctuary alone. What he heard, nobody knows. The priest greeted him as son of Amun, the ordinary title of every pharaoh. Plutarch tells a sweeter version: the priest tried to say my son in Greek, O paidion, stumbled, and it came out O pai Dios, son of Zeus. Alexander told his friends only that he had the answer he wanted, and wrote to his mother that he would tell her the secret in person. He never saw her again. After his death, coins showed him with the curled ram's horns of Ammon, and ancient writers say he wished to be buried here. Instead his body went to Alexandria and was lost. A Greek archaeologist claimed his tomb at Siwa in 1995, but experts rejected it. Now look at the sanctuary door: that is the threshold he crossed alone.

period: Late Period, 30th Dynasty, Nectanebo II, 360-343 BC
summary: Amun's second temple stood for over 2,000 years, until a local official blew it up in the 1890s for building stone. One wall survived.
look: A single tall wall of inscribed limestone standing among the palms, a short walk from the Aghurmi rock, which you can see from here. Face its decorated side: rows of gods carved in relief with columns of hieroglyphs. Loose blocks from the rest of the temple lie scattered around its base.
story:
Umm Ubayda was the second temple of Amun in the oasis, built by Nectanebo II, the last native Egyptian pharaoh, in the 4th century BC. It stood a short distance from the oracle temple at Aghurmi, and a straight processional road joined the two. On festival days, the Greek historian Diodorus says, about 80 priests carried the god's image in its sacred boat, women and girls sang hymns, and the boat answered questions by tilting.

European travellers saw the temple largely standing. William George Browne visited in 1792 and thought this was the oracle itself. Later visitors drew it. Then in the 1890s, most accounts say 1896, a local official, usually named as Mahmud Azmi, used explosives to break it up for building stone for the new town. What you see is what he left.

The surviving wall carries reliefs and inscriptions of Nectanebo II's reign, with a procession of gods. It is a small window onto how richly decorated the temples of Siwa once were.
details: The decorated face of the wall: a line of gods in relief; look for tall plumed crowns, the mark of Amun.
The columns of hieroglyphs between the figures, cut deep enough to catch the low sun.
The loose blocks around the base: pieces the explosives broke off and the builders left behind.
Turn toward the Aghurmi rock: the oracle temple at the other end of the old processional road.
fun_fact: William George Browne, the first European to describe Siwa since antiquity, saw this temple in 1792 and was sure he had found the famous oracle. He was a short walk off.
narration: This lonely wall is almost all that remains of Siwa's second temple of Amun, built by Nectanebo the Second, the last native Egyptian pharaoh, in the 4th century BC. It stood a short walk from the oracle temple on the Aghurmi rock, which you can see from here, and a straight processional road joined the two. On festival days, the Greek historian Diodorus says, about 80 priests carried the god in his sacred boat, women sang hymns, and the boat answered questions by dipping one way or the other. The temple survived more than 2,000 years. In 1792 the English traveller William George Browne saw it standing and thought it was the oracle itself. Then in the 1890s, most accounts say 1896, a local official blew it up with explosives to get building stone for the new town. One wall was left. Now look at its decorated face: you can still make out a line of gods carved in relief, a glimpse of how the interior once looked.

period: Late Period to Roman, from the 26th Dynasty onward
summary: A cone of rock riddled with tombs like a honeycomb, where Siwans hid from bombs in 1940 and found painted rooms unseen for some 2,000 years.
look: Gebel al-Mawta, the Mountain of the Dead, is a low limestone cone about 1 km north of the town centre, with rows of rock-cut tomb doors running round it in terraces. Most are plain, empty chambers; a guardian unlocks the few painted tombs, usually Si-Amun, Mesu-Isis, Niperpathot and the Crocodile. Climb to the top afterwards for the view over Shali and the palms.
story:
The hill was Siwa's cemetery for centuries, from the 26th Dynasty, when the oracle of Amun was at its most famous, through the Ptolemaic and Roman periods. Families cut tombs into its slopes, one row above another, many with several chambers and niches for the dead. Almost all were robbed in antiquity, and in some open chambers bones still lie where the robbers left them.

Then came the Second World War. In 1940 Italian aircraft bombed Siwa, and families moved into the old tombs for shelter. Clearing them out, they found painted walls. In the confusion some paintings were damaged, and some pieces were cut out and sold. The Egyptian archaeologist Ahmed Fakhry recorded what survived, and his work is still the basis of what we know.

The paintings show a mixed world. The gods are Egyptian: Osiris, Isis, Thoth, the sky goddess Nut. But some owners were Greek in taste, and the finest tomb shows its owner, Si-Amun, with curly hair and a beard in the Greek manner. Siwa was a frontier between Egypt, the Libyan desert and the Greek cities of Cyrenaica, and its dead were painted that way.

Come in the late afternoon. The painted tombs are dim anyway, and the top of the hill is one of the best sunset spots in the oasis.
details: The terraces of tomb doors cut round the hill: from the lower path, count how many levels you can see.
An open, unpainted tomb: look for burial niches cut into the walls, sometimes with bones still inside.
From the top, look south: Shali's melted mud town, and beyond it the palms running toward the salt lake.
On the slopes: scraps of ancient pottery. Leave them where they lie.
fun_fact: In 1940 the Mountain of the Dead briefly became a mountain of the living, with whole families sleeping in 2,000-year-old tombs to escape the air raids.
narration: This cone-shaped hill is Gebel al-Mawta, the Mountain of the Dead. Every dark doorway you can see is a tomb, cut into the rock in rows, one terrace above another. For centuries this was Siwa's cemetery, from the 26th Dynasty, when the oracle of Amun was at its most famous, through Greek and Roman times. Most tombs were robbed long ago, and many are plain chambers with niches for bodies. Some still have bones in them. The surprise came in 1940. During the Second World War, Italian planes bombed Siwa, and families took shelter in the old tombs. While clearing them out, they found painted walls that no one had seen for some 2,000 years. Some paintings were damaged in the rush, and some pieces were cut out and sold. The Egyptian archaeologist Ahmed Fakhry came to record what was left. The paintings show a mixed world. The gods are Egyptian, Osiris, Isis, Thoth and the sky goddess Nut, but some owners look Greek, with curly hair and beards. The guardian opens a few painted tombs, and Si-Amun's is the best. Afterwards, climb to the top and look south: the melted mud town of Shali sits in the middle of Siwa, with palms all the way to the salt lake.

period: Ptolemaic period, often dated to the 3rd century BC
summary: A Greek-looking man with curly hair and a beard, standing among Egyptian gods: Siwa's finest painted tomb is a portrait of a mixed world.
look: A rock-cut tomb on Gebel al-Mawta, its walls painted in strong reds, yellows and blues, with niches for burials. The owner appears among the gods of the dead, and the ceiling is painted as the sky. The guardian may restrict photography; flash is never allowed.
story:
Si-Amun means 'son of Amun', a fitting name in this oasis. We know nothing of his life beyond these walls. He was clearly rich, and the way he is painted, with dark curly hair and a full beard, suggests a man of Greek background, or at least Greek taste, who wanted an Egyptian afterlife. Most scholars place the tomb in the Ptolemaic period; the exact date is debated, and the 3rd century BC is often given.

The scenes are classic Egyptian funerary art. Si-Amun is shown with Osiris and the gods of the dead, among them the ibis-headed Thoth. In the classic descriptions, a goddess in a sycamore tree pours water for him, a promise that the dead will never thirst. Overhead, the ceiling is painted as the night sky, the domain of the sky goddess Nut.

There is also a family. Si-Amun appears with his wife and a boy, usually read as his son, a warm, almost domestic touch inside an Egyptian afterlife.

The tomb was rediscovered in 1940 by Siwans sheltering from Italian bombs. Some painted panels were hacked out and sold before Ahmed Fakhry could record it, and since then camera flashes, dust and breath have dulled the colours. That is why the guardian is strict.
details: Si-Amun himself: dark curly hair and a full beard, unlike the clean-shaven Egyptian figures around him.
The ceiling: painted as the sky over his burial, the realm of the goddess Nut.
The ibis-headed Thoth among the gods of the dead: the scribe god who records the verdict.
Damaged patches in the plaster: scars from 1940s looting and later wear. Keep your flash off.
fun_fact: The tomb owner's name, 'son of Amun', is exactly the title the oracle gave Alexander the Great in this same oasis.
narration: You are inside the tomb of Si-Amun, the finest painted tomb in Siwa. His name means son of Amun, and he must have been rich. We know nothing about him except what these walls say. Look at the man himself: dark curly hair and a full beard, not the clean-shaven look of an Egyptian official. Most scholars see a man of Greek background, or at least Greek taste, who wanted an Egyptian afterlife, and they date the tomb to the Ptolemaic period, perhaps the 3rd century BC. Around him are the gods of the dead: Osiris, the ibis-headed Thoth, and, in the classic descriptions, a goddess in a sycamore tree pouring water for him, so that he will never thirst. Overhead, the ceiling is painted as the sky. On these walls Si-Amun also appears with his family, and a boy, usually read as his son. The paintings were rediscovered in 1940, when Siwans hid in these tombs from Italian bombs. Some panels were cut out and sold before the archaeologist Ahmed Fakhry recorded them, and camera flashes have faded the rest, so please keep your flash off. Now find Si-Amun's face and notice the curls: a Greek face in an Egyptian heaven.
